title: Only Humanities Students Ask Good Questions
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Patrick Dempsey takes aim at a popular defense of the humanities in the AI era, built on Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark's remark that studying literature taught him to ask good questions. He first recasts the argument as a syllogism and exposes its selection bias and counterfactual problems: we see the exceptional literature graduate, not the denominator, and cannot know whether a different major would have produced the same person. He then questions whether ask good questions even has a stable meaning, noting that small children ask hundreds of questions a day, and challenges the lack of evidence that humanities courses develop this capacity uniquely. His sharpest move compares philosophy with economics, nursing and HVAC training, asking why humanities questioning is presumed to transfer to life and citizenship while vocational questioning is presumed to stay on the job site. He traces this assumption to a status hierarchy in which the philosophy graduate is called educated and the tradesperson merely skilled. He concedes the humanities may help some students ask better questions, but rejects any claim of uniqueness.
points: Dempsey frames the Jack Clark argument as a syllogism and identifies selection bias and a missing counterfactual as its core flaws.
He argues ask good questions is as vague as critical thinking and needs definition before anyone can claim to teach it.
The HVAC comparison exposes an unexamined assumption that humanities thinking transfers broadly while vocational thinking stays narrow.
He links the claim to a vocabulary of status in which some fields produce the educated and others merely the skilled.
quotes: We are being shown the literature graduate who became the billionaire co-founder of Anthropic precisely because he is exceptional. We are not shown the denominator
But “useful to Jack Clark” in no way entails “therefore young people should not turn away from the humanities because these subjects cultivate capacities required by the future.
Ask good questions” as a phrase is about as meaningless as “critical thinking” and is probably even less meaningful than saying “it is what it is.
So I do love the irony of higher education congratulating itself for teaching adults how to do something small children do compulsively

Why should the questions raised in Philosophy 101 be considered broadly transferable questions about life, judgment, and the human condition, while questions developed through HVAC work remain trapped inside an AC unit?
Don’t miss this point. We would never dare describe the master electrician with fifteen years of accumulated experience as highly educated!
But none of that entails the humanities does this uniquely or better than some alternative.
